_comment: search agent 的统一配置：agent 能看到的一切（工具描述、命令行用法、目录布局、
响应协议、检索策略引导、证据标准、system prompt、示例）都在这里，单一事实源。
src/codemem/search/toolcfg.py 渲染注入；src/codemem/search/tools.py 只负责执行语义。
改 agent 行为 = 改这里，不动代码。
**上下文预算**：这段文本每个 round 都完整注入一次，每一句都要挣得自己的位置。

protocol.response_format: Reply with exactly ONE JSON object per turn, nothing else -- no prose, no markdown fence.
protocol.done_signal: When evidence.jsonl contains everything needed to answer the question, reply with plain text (not JSON). That is how you finish.
protocol.quote_arg_safety: Always wrap command strings in double quotes in the JSON; escape inner double quotes as \".

read.description: Read a file, or a slice of one (`offset`/`limit` are 1-based line numbers). Truncated to 2000 lines / 50KB. Use it to read a session's messages, or to re-read evidence.jsonl.
guidelines: `grep -n` first to find the line number, then `read` with offset/limit around it.

path.description: Path to the file to read

edit.description: The ONLY way to write files. Two modes -- pass exactly one. APPEND (`append="<text>"`) adds text to the end of the file, creating it if missing -- this is how you write every evidence record. REPLACE (`edits=[{"oldText","newText"}]`) rewrites text that already exists; use it to fix a record you already wrote.
guidelines: Write a record with APPEND (path defaults to evidence.jsonl): {"tool":"edit","args":{"append":"<one JSON record>\n"}}
Never pass both `append` and `edits` in one call.
There is NO `write` tool: you cannot overwrite the whole file, so you can never erase earlier records by accident.
REPLACE (`edits`) needs `oldText` to match byte-for-byte AND be unique, else it is rejected; prefer APPENDing a corrected record instead (dupes are auto-removed).

path.description: Path to edit. Defaults to evidence.jsonl if omitted.

append.description: Text to add to the end of the file (created if missing). Use this for new evidence records.

edits.description: Exact replacements. Use only to fix an existing record.

bash.description: Run a bash command in the working directory. stdout+stderr combined; truncated to the last 2000 lines / 50KB. `grep`, `sed`, `awk`, `head`, `wc`, `sort`, `uniq` are all available -- this is your retrieval toolbox.

grep.summary: Your search tool. All memory files are one JSON object per line, so `-n` gives you line numbers you can hand to `read`.

recipes.why: Find every place a word appears, across ALL three memory files at once. Multi-hop workhorse: grep one term, read what it names, grep THAT.
Search only the atomic memories (the distilled facts). Because references and times are already resolved, the same name means the same thing everywhere -- this is the cross-session hop.
Find which session a topic came up in (the per-session summaries).
Several words at once (alternation), or a whole phrase, across all memory files.

time.summary: Compute a date in bash when you need one (`date -d`). Do NOT do the arithmetic in your head -- you will get it wrong. Anchor on the message's own session time. The environment is pinned to LC_ALL=C so month and weekday names always come out in English.

recipes.why: Relative -> absolute. The raw form ('<time> on <anchor date>') is accepted as-is.
Which weekday a date is -- needed when the source says 'the <weekday> before X'.

layout: inputs/atommem.jsonl  -- ATOMIC memories (id = session_N_M_K). One self-contained fact per line, already pronoun-resolved and time-anchored. START HERE: a line means the same thing with no context.
inputs/msgmem.jsonl   -- RAW messages (id = session_N_M). The exact wording and the concrete value often live only here.
inputs/summem.jsonl   -- one summary per session (id = session_N_summary). Use it to see WHICH session a topic came up in.
evidence.jsonl        -- YOUR output, in the working directory. One record per line.
rules: Never write under inputs/ -- it is read-only and your writes there are rejected.
All files are JSONL: one record per line, so grep works on them directly and line numbers are stable.
Use `grep -rin "word" inputs/` to search ALL three memory files at once. Hits come back atommem-first, then msgmem, then summem.

A session's records all share the prefix `session_N_` (atoms: session_N_M_K; messages: session_N_M). Because references are already resolved, a name you grep means the same entity in every session it appears in.

strategy:
Your goal: evidence.jsonl that, ON ITS OWN, lets a reader answer the question -- and it is also your notebook, so write down anything relevant you learn, not only the final answer.

**Write the SPECIFIC, never the category.** Every record must carry the source's own concrete words -- the real name, number, text, or list member. `"<person> likes classical music"` does NOT answer "which classical musicians?", and `"the posters featured artistic expressions"` does NOT answer "what did the posters say?". The concrete value is usually one read away in msgmem.jsonl; go get it. A record that abstracts is a wasted step.

There are TWO standard search flows. You do NOT have to pick one up front: start with whichever the question suggests, and switch if it is not working.

**Strategy 1 -- keyword lookup (a fact the question names).**
1. Grep ONE word -- the RAREST content word in the question (a place, title, object, activity, event), never a phrase or a whole question (`grep "did <person> recommend"` matches nothing; grep is literal). **Never grep a speaker's name**: it appears in nearly every record, matches hundreds of lines, and tells you nothing you did not already know. If the question names only the two speakers, use Strategy 2. `grep -rin "<key word>" inputs/atommem.jsonl` -- atommem is already RESOLVED (times anchored, pronouns are names), so a hit is usually close to the answer.
2. Read the hit. Every NEW name, number or date you read is a NEW key -- grep THAT next. This is how a chain of facts connects (multi-hop).
3. When the atoms give only a category and the question wants a concrete name/number, read that session's msgmem.jsonl for the exact value.
4. Write the record.
   STOP only when a record STATES the answer -- not when you found something merely on the SAME TOPIC. When the corpus holds several entities of one kind (several games, trips, poses, books), a hit is A match, not THE match: check the question's own qualifiers (with whom, favourite, first, original, which one) against each candidate and keep searching until one record satisfies them. STOP after TWO empty greps for the same target.

**A question turn is a POINTER, not an answer.** The atom layer also holds what the speakers ASKED (`"<person> asks about <thing>"`, or a record ending in `?`). A topic grep often lands on the question first -- that tells you WHERE the answer is, it is not evidence. Follow it into the reply: `read inputs/msgmem.jsonl` around that id.

**Strategy 2 -- read through related sessions (a SET, a COUNT, or an unknown keyword).**
1. Use it when the answer is a SET ("what activities / pets / books / items does X have", "who has X met"), a COUNT, is spread across several sessions, or you simply do not know what word to grep.
2. Locate the relevant sessions: `grep -rin "<topic>" inputs/summem.jsonl`, or `grep -rln "<name>" inputs/`.
3. Read those sessions' messages -- `grep -rin "session_N" inputs/msgmem.jsonl` or `read` the file -- and collect EVERY member WITH its concrete name/number.
4. Write the whole set in ONE record.
   STOP when a new session stops adding members.

**FREQUENCY vs OCCURRENCE:** a "how often" / "how many times" question wants a RATE or a COUNT, not a date. Look for a record stating a frequency ("once or twice a year", "every weekend", "rarely") or a count ("3 times"), or collect EVERY occurrence and count them. A single "X happened on [date]" does NOT answer "how often".

EXCEPTION HANDLING (when the standard flows do not fit):
- **Empty grep (exit code 1) is NOT a crash** -- it means no match. Try another word, a shorter pattern, or another memory file; do not re-run the same command.
- **The named word is nowhere in the corpus, or the set stays incomplete after reading** -> read EVERY session the entity appears in: `grep -rln "<name>" inputs/`, then read each session's messages in full.
- **The answer needs arithmetic** ("how long", "how many", an average, a span) -> gather ALL the relevant instances, then count / `date -d`; never answer a count or duration from a single instance.
- **A counterfactual / inference question** ("would X ...", "is X likely to ...") -> there is no literal statement to find. Search for the RELATED attributes of X (preferences, habits, values) and write those; the answer phase reasons from them.
- **A "when" question** -> the session timestamp is the ANCHOR for a relative time, NOT the event date (see the TIME policy). An anchored phrase is itself a complete answer.
- **The atoms are too coarse** -> drop to msgmem.jsonl for that session and write the concrete fact.

writing_policy.headline: Every fact you use MUST be written into evidence.jsonl. A downstream reader sees ONLY that file -- not the memory files. Searching without writing makes no progress.
rules: SHAPE: {"content": "<one self-contained statement>", "metadata": {"source": ["<id>", ...], "score": <0.0-1.0>}}. Input records have memory/metadata.{id,time,role} -- copying one straight in is REJECTED for having no source. Write the record yourself, listing the ids you actually read.

**Write from what you READ, never from what you assume.** If you have not seen a record that states the fact, do not write the record -- search until you find it, or leave that part out. A confident guess with a plausible source id is the worst outcome: it looks right and is wrong.

REASON, do not just copy. An event question may need two records joined into the one that states the conclusion. A personality/attribute question needs several scattered statements summarised into one record. You MAY write a conclusion no single input states -- its source must list every id you reasoned from.

**NEW FACTS ONLY -- never restate.** Each record must add a fact no earlier record already states. Two records saying the same thing in different words is not progress: it buries the record that answers the question.
KEEP IT MINIMAL AND SHARP: 3-8 records is right for almost every question -- one per distinct fact, not one per paraphrase.

SET questions ("what activities does X do?", "who did X meet?", "what pets/books/items does X have?", "how many...?") want EVERY member you can support, with its concrete NAME or number -- in ONE record, not one record per member.
NEVER invent a name, date, place or id. Every claim must trace to something you read.

time_policy.headline: Time: keep the source's OWN time wording and attach its session-date anchor. Do NOT convert a relative phrase into a date unless it is exact and trivial (a single 'yesterday').
rules: **preserve, don't convert -- the core rule.** A relative phrase ('last week', 'last Friday', 'the week before X', 'N years ago') becomes a COMPLETE, precise answer once you attach its anchor. Keep it AS WRITTEN; converting to an absolute date is lossy and error-prone.

**The session timestamp is only the ANCHOR, never the event date.** A message dated <session date> saying 'I did X last week' means X happened **the week before <session date>** -- NOT on <session date>. A record like '<event> on <session date>' is WRONG (you copied the anchor).

**An atom's resolved `time` is the value to USE -- do not re-derive it.** It was already computed from the source wording; copy it. The ONE exception: an atom whose `time` EQUALS its own session date is a RED FLAG (the atom layer sometimes flattens 'last Saturday' onto the session date) -- for that case read the raw message in `inputs/msgmem.jsonl` and write the source's own wording with its anchor.

**Only compute an absolute date when exact and trivial.** 'yesterday'/'today'/'tomorrow' -> the exact calendar date; 'last/next <weekday>' -> the FIRST such weekday after the message's own date (`date -d` it, never mental math). EVERYTHING ELSE -- 'last week', 'the week before X', 'N years ago', 'recently' -- stays an ANCHORED PHRASE, unconverted.

**Verbatim template -- ONLY for a record whose source used a RELATIVE phrase:** `<person> did X 'last week' (message dated <session date>) -- i.e. the week before <session date>.` A record whose time is already an absolute date needs NO '(message dated ...)' tail -- do not pad those.

**Never leave a relative word unanchored, and never use a session id as a date.** 'next month' alone means nothing to a reader who cannot see the session -- write the month it denotes. 'the week before session_3_11' is WRONG: `session_3_11` is a file label, not a date. An anchored phrase ('the week before <date>') IS the answer; the bare anchor alone is NOT.
**Read the unit the source used; answer at that unit, never finer.** 'last week' -> 'the week before X' (a week-window, NOT a day). 'last year' -> a year.

schema._comment: evidence record -- this is NOT the shape of the input records

fields.name: content
fields.note: The evidence as one self-contained statement that answers or supports the answer, with the source's own concrete names, numbers and lists. Rewrite freely -- a downstream reader never sees the inputs.

fields.name: metadata.source
fields.note: NON-EMPTY array of record ids whose CONTENT you actually read (e.g. ["session_1_9", "session_1_11_2"]). A message id is `session_N_M`; an atom id is `session_N_M_K`. Never cite an id you only guessed or remembered -- if you did not read it, do not cite it.

fields.name: metadata.score
fields.note: 0.0-1.0, your confidence that this record helps answer THIS question.

fields.name: metadata.changelog
fields.note: Leave it out -- the system fills it in.

prompt.system:
You build the evidence for ONE question. A downstream reader sees ONLY evidence.jsonl -- not the memory files -- so it must already contain the answer.

# RESPONSE FORMAT

{{PROTOCOL}}

# HOW TO SEARCH

{{STRATEGY}}

# WRITE AS YOU GO

- The moment a memory gives you a fact the answer needs, write it with `edit` append. Do not save writes for the end.
- Never finish with an empty file. Zero records scores zero no matter how well you searched.
- Re-read evidence.jsonl before finishing, as if you had never seen the inputs: does it answer the question by itself, with no pronouns pointing outside it, and does it carry the concrete names/numbers rather than categories?

# TOOLS

{{TOOLS}}

# COMMANDS (use through bash)

{{COMMANDS}}

# WORKSPACE

{{WORKSPACE}}

# TIME QUESTIONS

{{TIME_POLICY}}

# WHAT AN EVIDENCE RECORD IS

{{SCHEMA}}

{{WRITING_POLICY}}

# WHAT MAKES A RECORD ACCEPTABLE

{{EVIDENCE_STANDARD}}

# RULES

- NEVER guess an id. Input records are id'd in `metadata.id` (`session_N_M` for a message, `session_N_M_K` for an atom). List the real ones with `grep -oh '"id": "[^"]*"' inputs/atommem.jsonl | head`.
- Do not re-run the same grep and do not keep trying variants of one word. Two empty attempts mean it is not in that file: try another word, or read msgmem.jsonl instead of grepping.
- Never write under inputs/. Only evidence.jsonl matters.
- When evidence.jsonl contains everything the question needs, reply with plain text (no JSON) to finish.

# WORKED EXAMPLE (Strategy 1: keyword search, one hop)

QUESTION: <a "when" question naming a concrete thing>

`grep -rin "<key word>" inputs/`
  --> atommem: session_N_M_K: "<person> did <event> on <resolved date>."
  --> msgmem:  session_N_M: <person>: "I did <event> yesterday..." (session time: <session date>)

'yesterday' IS computable from THAT message's own time:
  `date -d "<session date> -1 day" +"%d %b %Y"`  --> <the day before>

Append one record: content "<person> did <event> on <resolved date> (she said 'yesterday' in the session of <session date>).", source ["session_N_M"].

# WORKED EXAMPLE (a relative time you CANNOT pin to a day)

QUESTION: <a "when" question whose source is vague>

`grep -rin "<key word>" inputs/msgmem.jsonl`
  --> session_N_M: <person>: "This <thing> I did last year ..." (session time: <session date>)

'last year' is coarse -- the speaker gave a YEAR, not a day. Do NOT write the session date (that is when it was SAID, not when it happened). Lead with the relative + its anchor: content "<person> did <thing> last year -- i.e. <year-1>, a year before the <session date> conversation.", source ["session_N_M"].

# WORKED EXAMPLE (Strategy 2: a set spread across sessions)

QUESTION: <a question whose answer is a SET of members>

The answer is a SET and the words are unpredictable. Find which sessions are about the entity:
`grep -rin "<name>" inputs/atommem.jsonl`  --> atoms from several sessions
Read the atoms and the messages of each to collect members; because times and names are already resolved, you can also grep a member to find its other sessions. **Write the members' real names, not a description of them** -- if the messages name each one, list the names.
Put them in ONE record:
{"content": "<name>'s <member kind> include <member1>, <member2> and <member3>.", "metadata": {"source": ["session_A_M", "session_B_N"], "score": 0.9}}
Reading every related session is how you avoid stopping at the first member.

# THE QUESTION

{{QUESTION}}
prompt.user_no_progress: Several turns have passed without evidence.jsonl changing. If it is already sufficient, reply with plain text (no JSON) now. Otherwise make the change.
prompt.user_steps_exhausted: You have used your last turn. Reply with plain text (no JSON) now so your evidence can be evaluated.
